narrationSegments.text: Put a ring around Earth like Saturn's, and a kid opening the curtains would see a stripe across the sky.

shots.visual: Set: V1: Today's Earth floating in space; rocks close in from a wider orbit and settle into a ring around it.; V2: Bedroom, foreground curtains. A kid pulls the curtains open with both hands; bright window.; V3: Outside the window: a pale stripe cuts across a blue sky; the kid looks up (POSE-KID-LOOK-UP).

narrationSegments.text: At the equator, the ring is a thin line straight overhead.
Farther north, it stretches into a wide arch.
Far enough north, it never rises above the horizon.

shots.visual: Set: V1: Equator beach, palm fronds in the foreground. The ring is a thin bright line straight overhead.; V2: The kid on the sand looks straight up (POSE-KID-LOOK-UP); the thin line passes right above.; V3: Mid-latitude city rooftop, railing in the foreground. The ring is a wide arch over the southern sky; the kid sweeps an arm along it.; V4: The arch comes down to the horizon over the rooftops.; V5: Far-north snowy town, fence and snow bank in the foreground. The sky is empty.; V6: A faint dotted line marks where the ring would be below the horizon; the kid shrugs (POSE-KID-SHRUG).

characters.action: Looks straight up at the equator, sweeps an arm along the arch, then shrugs (POSE-KID-SHRUG) in the far north.

characterMotion.action: Poses swap instantly and are held at least 2 frames; the camera does most of the acting.

narrationSegments.text: A study suggests that 466 million years ago, an asteroid passed too close, and Earth's pull tore it apart into a ring.

shots.visual: Set: V1: An in-world paper with the stamp 'A STUDY SUGGESTS' (a hypothesis, not a fact); the globe turns behind it.; V2: A timeline card slides back to '466 MILLION YEARS AGO' over a plain ancient globe.; V3: A lumpy asteroid sails toward Earth, passing close; foreground rock fragments streak past.; V4: The asteroid stretches, cracks and splits; the pieces spiral into a ring around the globe; warm glow at the break.

characterMotion.action: Poses swap instantly and are held at least 2 frames; the camera does most of the acting.

narrationSegments.text: You see, a ring doesn't last forever.
Its pieces slowly fall back, and near the equator is where they'd land.

narrationSegments.text: Some experts doubt the crater ages, but if the study is right, Earth once wore a ring, long before the dinosaurs.

A small trilobite looks up through shallow water at a ring arching across the sky.; V4: The ring fades out; a small cartoon dinosaur walks in under an empty sky and looks up.
